The pork industry rejects the term "factory farm," insisting that family farmers raise pigs just like they always have.

But 50 years ago this month, in September 1976, Hog Farm Management magazine wrote: "Forget the pig is an animal. Treat him just like a machine in a factory."

That was the plan. And they acted on it: they soon moved pregnant sows into gestation crates and grower pigs into giant dark warehouses.

In 1976, most US pigs were on small farms with fewer than 500 pigs. Today most are in factory farms with more than 5,000. The consolidation put roughly 90% of US pig farmers out of business.

The promise was that industrialization would dramatically lower pork prices. But, in real terms, pork costs about the same today as it did in the 1970s.

The farmers got bankrupted and the pigs got crated. Only the factory farming corporations won.

Factory farmers have long claimed that economics force them to treat their animals well — crowd them too much and they won't thrive.

A newish study (Rabiul Awal et al., 2025) shows why this logic fails. It tested farming a species of small catfish at three different stocking densities.

Individual catfish did best at the lowest density.

But collective profits were maximized at the highest density — 1,330 fish per cubic meter — because the extra fish more than compensated for the higher death rate.

The study concluded that the "ideal density" for farming this species of catfish is 1,330 fish per cubic meter.

This is the economic logic of factory farming.

And it could spare tens of billions more from the sub-lethal suffering of lives of chronic pain, constantly on the brink of collapse.

I doubt the reps who voted for the farm bill knew it would do this. But they knew it would wipe out state crate bans. And they didn't care enough to ask what else would go with them.

In a world that often feels deeply polarized, it is rare to find a topic where almost everyone agrees. The treatment of farm animals is one of them.

Surveys across many countries show that a strong majority of people, regardless of their diet, oppose common practices in animal agriculture. In the chart you can see survey data from the UK.

Given these surveys, and with the increasing availability of plant-based meat alternatives, one might expect people in these countries to be shifting away from consuming animal products.

But the data shows a different story.

At a global level, meat consumption is not only high but also increasing. Each year, hundreds of billions of land animals, fish, and crustaceans are farmed and killed to produce food.

There is a clear gap between what people want — meat produced without suffering — and what the food system delivers. Understanding this gap is the first step to closing it.

In a new article, Pablo Rosado makes the case that one of the biggest opportunities of our generation is to build a system where the food we eat reflects the values we already hold.

Great to see IHOP and Applebee's announce they're now sourcing 100% cage-free eggs.

Battery cages are among the crueler things we've invented. They confine hens so tightly they can't even spread their wings — for their entire lives.

Cage-free isn't perfect. But it at least lets hens move, perch, nest, and dustbathe — their most basic natural behaviors.

IHOP and Applebee's move alone will spare about a million hens from lives in overcrowded cages.

Most major food companies pledged to go cage-free years ago. Many still haven't. It's time to make good.

2042284906383028697.text:
Almost all male piglets on US factory farms are castrated with a non-sterile knife or scalpel.

The industry calls it 'surgical castration.' But there's no vet, anesthetic, or pain relief involved.

Anesthesia would cost about five cents per piglet. Pain relief would cost one cent. 

France and Germany already require anesthesia. Brazil's pork industry is phasing out castration altogether.

The US pork industry doesn't think it's worth the cost.

Photo: Andrew Skowron / We Animals

2041559856042463500.text:
The 'eat less red meat' advice may have done more harm to animals than any other nutrition recommendation.

Fifty years ago, Americans ate 95 pounds of beef and 40 pounds of chicken annually. Then doctors started telling people to replace red meat with white meat.

Americans complied: today we eat 37% less beef — and 165% more chicken. 

US slaughterhouses now kill 15 million fewer cattle each year — and over 5 billion more chickens. (Population growth only explains a third of that increase.)

And the chickens have it much worse. US beef cattle spend 70–85% of their lives out on the range. Almost all chickens spend their entire lives atop a pile of manure in a dimly-lit factory farm.

2041204854606250334.text:
In 2023, Chinese researchers set out to create a 'pig depression model' — a way to reliably induce depression in pigs for medical research. 

The researchers (Yang et al, 2023) confined pigs so tightly they couldn't move and left them in a dark environment without food or water for 24 hours.

It worked: the pigs exhibited anhedonia — an inability to experience pleasure — along with anxiety and reduced appetite. The researchers concluded they'd found a promising way to induce depression in pigs.

Their inspiration? Factory farms. They tried out the total restraint after noting that sows, confined in gestation crates and kept chronically hunger, "have been found to be in a depression-like state."

The main difference? After 24 hours, the researchers let the study pigs out. On factory farms they never do.

Photo: Balvik C. / We Animals

2039024707140284499.text:
Why is US chicken so cheap? One trick: our factory farms don't remove waste between flocks. New chicks are placed on years of built-up manure, feathers, and the remains of dead birds from previous flocks.

In Europe, this is illegal. Farms must remove all litter and lay fresh bedding before every new flock. The US has no such rule.

In parts of Mississippi and the Delmarva Peninsula, some chicken houses haven't been fully cleaned out in 10+ years.

The result: US chickens get necrotic ulcers on their feet from standing in wet, ammonia-soaked litter — and chemical burns on their chests from lying in the waste they live on.

And you get slightly cheaper 'all-natural' chicken.

2038677205795164276.text:
You've heard about the provision to keep pigs in gestation crates hidden in the farm bill. Turns out there's another anti-animal provision buried in there too.

Section 3201(d) would repeal a 30-year-old law barring federal tax dollars from funding mink fur industry marketing. Mink are wild, solitary animals. On fur factory farms, they're crammed into cages where they routinely attack each other.

Americans don't want factory-farmed fur. So the farm bill would use our tax dollars to subsidize marketing mink fur to wealthy consumers abroad — primarily in China.

Politicians know animal welfare is more popular than this kind of corporate welfare. So they buried this in the farm bill's trade section — in a line that doesn't even mention 'fur.'

This isn't a farm bill anymore. It's a factory farm bill. There's still time to tell your senators and representatives to stop it.

Photo credit: Jo-Anne McArthur, WeAnimals.

2036861569695703200.text:
Just found this wild detail in the special prosecutor's report on the beagle cruelty case at Ridglan Farms in Wisconsin.

The prosecutor found clear evidence of criminal cruelty — including employees cutting out parts of dogs' eyes without pain relief or veterinary care (he euphemistically called this the 'cherry-eye procedure').

But he declined to prosecute, in part after speaking with local factory farmers who told him they had 'different views' about animal mistreatment.

After speaking with them, he concluded that 'the reality is that the Ridglan Farms business model was not unusual.'

Of course, 'different views' and industry norms are not legal defenses to animal cruelty. So he called them 'equity considerations.' In other words, it would be unfair to prosecute these animal abusers because their neighbors also abuse animals.

2036090497421435154.text:
Scientists once trained chickens to choose between two feeds — one laced with pain relief. The lame ones chose significantly more of it than healthy birds (Danbury, 2000). They were self-medicating.

This is one of those lame chickens. I took this photo on a factory farm in India — but it could be anywhere. Most chickens globally come from just two breeds: the Cobb 500 and the Ross 708.

By five weeks old, up to 39% of these 'broiler' chickens are lame (Dixon, 2020). Not because of disease or accidents — because we've bred them to grow four times faster than natural. Their bodies can't keep up.

The genetics labs selected relentlessly for this rapid growth. The reward was slightly cheaper chicken.

They didn't bother to select for legs and organs that could keep pace. The price was chronic pain for billions of animals.

2034691418565091796.text:
This is a pig who spent years confined in a gestation crate. She was left behind when factory farms flooded in Iowa and then rescued by some volunteers.

The volunteers took her home and dug her a mud pit. She ignored it. They assumed years of confinement had extinguished her natural instincts.

Then they noticed her wandering into the woods on their property. They followed her — and found her rooting in a pile of dirt, digging her own mud pit.

The pork industry claims pigs adapt to confinement. They don't. Inside every gestation crate is an animal who still yearns to root, wallow, and just be a pig.

This is the tragedy of factory farming. We tried to reduce feeling animals to machines. We failed.

2034311814453023108.text:
Pigs don't just feel fear themselves. They also feel the fear of other pigs — and try to comfort them.

In one study, pigs watching another pig in distress first showed fear themselves and then tried to comfort the distressed pig through snout-to-snout contact. Pigs who'd previously endured the same ordeal reacted even more intensely — they seemed to recognize what the distressed pig was going through. (Goumon & Špinka, 2016.) 

On factory farms, pigs trapped in gestation crates aren't just feeling afraid themselves. They're feeling the fear of all the other pigs around them. But the crate's iron bars stop them from even turning toward their fellow pigs — let alone comforting them with their snout.

2033974595645280264.text:
Finally, someone is willing to defend the farm bill's gestation crate provision.

Its co-sponsor Rep. Feenstra says it's necessary to 'protect family farms.' But when family farmers came to Congress to testify against this very provision, Feenstra and his colleagues refused to let them speak.

Oklahoma pig farmers Leo Staples and Nate Beaulac went to Washington to fight it — and were met with a wall of lobbyists and money. Many more family farmers, like Joel Salatin, Brent Hershey, and Russ Kremer, have spoken out against it too. Feenstra has ignored them all.

Feenstra says he doesn't want 'one state dictating how farmers raise livestock.' So instead he'll let two foreign-owned corporations — Smithfield and JBS — dictate it for every state.

He says this will 'restore common sense to agricultural policy.' Only in lobbyist-filled backrooms does wiping out basic state anti-cruelty laws count as 'common sense.'

2031442184105546034.text:
Glad to see this go viral — especially among conservatives. This fight isn't left vs. right. It's voters vs. lobbyists.

A lot of people are asking how this got into the farm bill. The answer: House Ag Chair Glenn Thompson put it in. Small farmers in his own district — who don't use crates — urged him not to. He said he didn't care: the National Pork Producers Council wanted it.

Principled conservatives like Reps. Anna Paulina Luna, David Valadao, Nancy Mace, Brian Fitzpatrick, and Thomas Massie have strongly opposed this provision. But too many Congressional Republicans have fallen in line with the industrial pork lobby.

The farm bill still has to pass the full House, then the Senate, where it needs 60 votes. It'll be a close vote, so every vote will matter.

Call 202-224-3121, select your reps and senators, and tell them: oppose the farm bill if the Save Our Bacon Act stays in. We can stop this.

Rebranded the 'Save Our Bacon Act,' it's a pork-industry play to wipe out every state law banning the sale of pork from crated pigs — laws the conservative Supreme Court upheld in 2023.

Over 85% of Democrats and Republicans oppose these crates. Voters have backed ballot measures to ban them in state after state.

2028951289967853600.text:
US supermarket giant Ahold Delhaize (Food Lion, Giant, Stop & Shop) is taking major new steps to eliminate cages from its supply chain.

A decade ago, most top US food companies pledged to end gestation crates for pigs and battery cages for hens — extreme confinement systems that 85%+ of Americans oppose. 

Many followed through. Costco and McDonald's are now almost entirely cage-free and crate-free, which they've achieved without raising prices.

But the five biggest US supermarket owners — Walmart, Kroger, Albertsons, Ahold Delhaize, and Aldi — all missed their 2025 cage-free deadlines.

Ahold was amongst the worst. It insisted it would now go cage-free by 2032 but refused to share any plans or progress. (We now know it was at just 25% cage-free.)

Advocates spent the past year educating Ahold’s customers about the reality behind the eggs it sells under labels like “farm fresh” (none disclose that they're from caged animals).

Today Ahold reversed course. It published clear milestones to reach 100% cage-free eggs — and reported significant progress on eliminating gestation crates.

Of course, these changes should have happened years ago. It shouldn't have required a campaign for Ahold to fulfill its own animal welfare policies.

But this is real progress. It will spare millions of hens and pigs from a lifetime in immobilizing cages and crates.

Huge credit to the advocates who held Ahold accountable and made this happen. Now it's time for Walmart, Kroger, Albertsons, and Aldi to follow suit.

2028486234671071562.text:
KFC, Nando's, and other top UK fast food chains just scrapped their pledges to stop using "Frankenchickens."

Their excuse? The climate.

They claim switching to higher-welfare breeds would raise emissions. And it's true — Frankenchickens do emit less. You can’t burn energy moving if you’re too lame to walk.

But the difference is tiny. Adopting the full Better Chicken Commitment — including phasing out Frankenchickens — would increase emissions by just 11% (Van Horne et al., 2025). 

That’s ~0.5 kg CO₂ per chicken — equivalent to about one bite of steak or 30 seconds of flying. On carbon markets, they could have offset this for ~3 pence (4 cents) per chicken.

Meanwhile, the animal welfare reforms they abandoned would spare each chicken 100+ hours of “hurtful” and “disabling” pain over their short lives (Welfare Footprint Project, 2022).

So either Nando’s, KFC, and the others are terrible at scope-sensitive trade-offs — or this was never really about the climate.

2019832871054426338.text:
Counterintuitively, rising beef prices are bad news for animals.

People buy more chicken when beef costs more. 

It takes ~200X more chickens to produce the same amount of meat as one cow -- and those chickens endure far worse conditions on factory farms.
